A banded stone of red (sard) and white (onyx) layers, highly prized in Rome for signet rings and cameos (Pliny, Natural History 37); Scipio Africanus is said to have been the first Roman to wear one.
Associated with sealing and engraving, it may fit the theme of God's people bearing his name. Its exact identity is reasonably secure but its symbolic value is uncertain.
The sixth, carnelian
Sardion was the first stone of the breastpiece (Exodus 28:17 Septuagint) and appears in Ezekiel 28:13. The One on the throne looked like jasper and carnelian (Revelation 4:3).
The name sardion is traditionally connected with Sardis, one of the seven churches (3:1-6). Reddish carnelian was the commonest stone for Roman engraved signet gems.
A blood-red or flesh-coloured stone that, with jasper, describes God's appearance in 4:3; its presence ties the foundations again to the throne vision.
The seventh, chrysolite

Chrysolithos is the tenth breastpiece stone in the Septuagint (Exodus 28:20, Hebrew tarshish) and appears in Ezekiel 28:13; Ezekiel's wheels (Ezekiel 1:16; 10:9) and Daniel's heavenly man's body (Daniel 10:6) gleam like tarshish.

Literally 'gold-stone': a golden-yellow gem, perhaps yellow topaz or citrine; Pliny (37.126) mentions chrysolites from India and Ethiopia. Ancient and modern names do not coincide (modern 'chrysolite' is olivine).
Its golden colour matches the gold city; its association with heavenly beings in Ezekiel and Daniel adds to the city's heavenly character.
The eighth, beryl
Bēryllion is the eleventh breastpiece stone in the Septuagint (Exodus 28:20) and appears in Ezekiel 28:13 Septuagint.
A sea-green to blue-green stone; Pliny (Natural History 37) says the best beryls came from India and that lapidaries cut them into hexagonal shapes to enhance their brilliance.
Adds sea-green brilliance; any further symbolism is uncertain.
The ninth, topaz

Topazion is the second breastpiece stone in the Septuagint (Exodus 28:17, Hebrew pitdah); Job 28:19 says the topaz of Cush cannot equal wisdom; Ezekiel 28:13 lists it in Eden; Psalm 119:127 (Septuagint) values God's commands above topaz.
Pliny (Natural History 37) says topazos came from an island in the Red Sea, and describes a greenish stone — probably what is now called peridot rather than modern topaz.
In Job it represents the most precious earthly wealth, which cannot buy wisdom; in the city it is simply part of the foundation, showing what God gives freely.
The tenth, chrysoprase
Not in the breastpiece lists or anywhere else in the Bible; another of John's additions.
From 'gold' and 'leek': an apple-green or golden-green stone, perhaps the green chalcedony now called chrysoprase; Pliny mentions chrysoprasus from India (Natural History 37).
Adds to the variety of colour and the sense of a city built of every precious stone known; no specific symbolism is established.
The eleventh, jacinth

Hyakinthos does not appear in the Septuagint breastpiece list, but some identify it with the Hebrew leshem, the seventh stone (Exodus 28:19; 'ligure' in the KJV, ligurion in the Septuagint). The colour 'hyacinth' (dark blue-violet) was used for the tabernacle curtains and priestly robes (Exodus 26:1; 28:31 Septuagint).
A blue-violet stone named after the hyacinth flower, possibly sapphire or blue zircon; Pliny (Natural History 37) describes it as a violet stone that quickly loses its lustre.
The colour of the tabernacle and priestly garments, reinforcing the city's priestly identity; the same colour is used for the demonic cavalry's breastplates in 9:17, now redeemed into holiness.
The twelfth, amethyst
Amethystos is the ninth breastpiece stone in the Septuagint (Exodus 28:19, Hebrew achlamah).
The Greek name means 'not intoxicated'; the stone was popularly believed to protect against drunkenness (Pliny, Natural History 37, reports and doubts such claims). Its purple matched royal dye.

A royal purple stone. Some commentators note the contrast with Babylon, who made the nations drunk with the wine of her immorality (14:8; 17:2) — the bride-city is sober and holy — though this is a suggestive rather than certain link.
The twelve gates were twelve pearls, each gate a single pearl

Isaiah 54:12 promises gates of sparkling jewels. A later rabbinic tradition attributed to Rabbi Yohanan (Babylonian Talmud, Baba Batra 75a; Sanhedrin 100a) says God will set up in Jerusalem's gates enormous pearls and precious stones hollowed out to form gateways — late, but showing the same imaginative tradition.

Pearls were the most valuable luxury in Rome (Pliny, Natural History 9, ranks them first among all valuables); Cleopatra is said to have dissolved a priceless pearl in vinegar, and Lollia Paulina paraded jewels worth forty million sesterces. The harlot is adorned with pearls (17:4) and they are among Babylon's cargo (18:12, 16).
What Babylon flaunted as status is here the common material of gates open to all. Jesus' parable of the pearl of great price (Matthew 13:45-46) may add that the kingdom is worth everything.
I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple

Ezekiel's visionary city centres on a rebuilt temple (Ezekiel 40-48), as do the Qumran Temple Scroll and New Jerusalem texts and Tobit 14:5. Jeremiah 3:16-17 foresees a day when the ark will no longer be remembered and Jerusalem itself will be called the throne of the LORD. 1 Enoch 90:28-29 replaces the old house with a new one.
Every Greco-Roman city's identity was tied to its temples — Ephesus to Artemis, Pergamum to Zeus, Athena and Augustus. A city with no temple would have been unthinkable.

A startling departure from Jewish expectation: the whole city is God's sanctuary (it is a cube like the Holy of Holies), and God's unmediated presence replaces any building. John 2:19-21 and 4:21-24 point the same way.
Dispensationalists distinguish the millennial age, in which they expect Ezekiel's temple to be literally built and used, from the eternal state described here, in which no temple is needed.

Amillennialists (Beale) see Ezekiel 40-48 fulfilled in this vision: the temple promises reach their goal in God and the Lamb dwelling with the people throughout the new creation, not in a future earthly building.
Partial preterists emphasise that after AD 70 no temple-centred worship remains; the church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21) is the reality the city depicts, perfected at the end.
No need of sun or moon… the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp; no night there

Isaiah 60:19-20: the sun will no longer be your light, for the LORD will be your everlasting light. Zechariah 14:7: continuous day, with no night. The menorah lamp of the tabernacle burned perpetually before God (Exodus 27:20-21).
Sun and moon were worshipped as deities (Helios/Sol, Selene/Luna), and emperors associated themselves with Sol. City gates were shut at nightfall for safety.
God's own glory replaces created light; the Lamb is the lamp that holds and spreads it. No night means no danger, no darkness of evil — so the gates never need to be shut.
By its light the nations will walk, and into it the kings of the earth will bring their glory

Isaiah 60:3-11: nations come to Zion's light, kings to the brightness of her dawn, bringing their wealth through gates open day and night. Psalm 72:10-11; Isaiah 2:2-4; Haggai 2:7 (the treasures of all nations shall come). Tobit 13:11 and 14:6 foresee nations turning to God and bringing gifts.
Client kings and provinces brought tribute and gifts to Rome; Rome drew the wealth of the nations to itself (18:11-17). In the new city, nations bring their glory freely to God.

The 'kings of the earth', elsewhere in Revelation allied with the beast (17:2; 19:19), now bring their glory into the city. Interpreters debate whether this speaks of the redeemed from all nations, the redemption of cultural achievements, or (in a minority view) a wide or universal salvation; Bauckham calls the conversion of the nations a major theme of the book.
Postmillennialists see the fulfilment of the Isaianic hope of converted nations, with Christianised peoples and their cultures offered to God — a goal already being realised in history.
Dispensationalists usually see distinct nations continuing in the eternal state, with Israel and the Gentile nations retaining their identity under God.
Amillennialists such as Hoekema stress that the best of human culture, purified, will be carried into the new earth by the redeemed of every nation.
Idealists read the nations and kings as the redeemed from every people now honouring God, the reversal of the world's allegiance to Babylon.
Nothing unclean will ever enter it… only those whose names are written in the Lamb's Book of Life

Isaiah 52:1: the uncircumcised and unclean will no longer enter Jerusalem; Isaiah 35:8 (the Way of Holiness); Zechariah 14:21 (no more trader in the house of the LORD). Temple purity laws barred the unclean from the sanctuary (Leviticus 15; Numbers 5:2-3).
Herod's temple carried warning inscriptions forbidding Gentiles to pass the barrier on pain of death; two have been found.
Holiness, not ethnicity, governs entry: the whole city is a sanctuary, and the only qualification is belonging to the Lamb. The open gates (21:25) and the exclusion of the unclean stand together.

Partial preterists such as Chilton read 21:1-22:5 as a portrait of the new covenant church, the bride that replaced apostate Jerusalem when the old order passed away in AD 70 — already the dwelling of God, healing the nations — while awaiting its final consummation at Christ's return. Gentry and others in the school affirm both this present dimension and a future, physical new creation.

Full preterists see the new heaven and earth and the new Jerusalem as the fully established new covenant world after AD 70, present now for believers; there is no future cosmic renewal. Critics note that this redefines the physical promises of Romans 8 and 2 Peter 3 and stands outside creedal orthodoxy; proponents argue that 'heaven and earth' in prophetic language often means the covenant order.

Historicists generally see chapters 21-22 as the eternal state following the millennium and final judgment, the climax of the church's long history depicted in earlier chapters; some saw partial anticipations in the gospel's spread.

Futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) see the eternal state after the millennium: a literal new earth and a literal city of the stated dimensions and materials. Dispensationalists distinguish the church's heavenly hope from Israel's earthly promises while seeing both united in the city with tribes and apostles.

Idealists (Hendriksen) see the ultimate destiny of the church, also partly realised wherever God dwells among his people now: holiness, beauty, security and unbroken fellowship with God. The city's cube shape (like the Holy of Holies), its gates named for Israel's tribes and foundations named for the apostles, and its point-by-point contrast with Babylon picture the one people of God as the temple filled with his presence.

Eclectic commentators (Osborne, Koester, Bauckham's theological reading) emphasise the symbolic and intertextual richness — Eden, tabernacle, temple and Zion fulfilled — and the city's contrast with Babylon, while affirming a future new creation.

Amillennialists see this as the consummation immediately following the single return of Christ and final judgment: the whole new earth as God's temple, fulfilling Ezekiel 40-48 and Isaiah 60-66 without any intervening earthly kingdom.

Postmillennialists also see the final state after Christ's return but often stress continuity with the gospel's historical victories: the nations' glory brought in is the harvest of the Great Commission.
Dispensational premillennialists see the eternal state after the millennium; some (Pentecost) hold the city already exists above the earth during the millennium as the home of glorified saints.
How does the bride-city of chapter 21 answer, point by point, the harlot-city of chapters 17-18?
What does it mean that the city has no temple? How does that relate to Ezekiel 40-48 and to John 2:19-21?
Is the New Jerusalem a place, a people, or both? What difference does Gundry's 'people as place' reading make?
Why do you think John borrows the high priest's breastpiece for the foundations of the city?
Who are the 'kings of the earth' who bring their glory into the city, given what Revelation says of them earlier?
The River and Tree of Life; 'Behold, I Am Coming Soon'
The new creation (22:1-5) and the epilogue (22:6-21)

The vision of the New Jerusalem closes with Eden restored: a crystal river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the city's main street, and the tree of life stands on either side, bearing twelve crops a year, its leaves for the healing of the nations. The curse is gone, God's servants see his face and bear his name on their foreheads, and they reign forever in his light. The epilogue then authenticates the whole book: the words are faithful and true, the time is near, the prophecy must not be sealed, and Jesus three times declares 'I am coming soon'. John again falls before the angel and is told to worship God; blessings are pronounced on those who keep the prophecy and wash their robes, and those who love falsehood remain outside. Jesus names himself the Root and Offspring of David and the bright Morning Star; the Spirit and the bride invite all who are thirsty; a solemn warning guards the book's words; and the church answers his promise with 'Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!'
The river of the water of life and the tree of life
No more curse: God's servants see his face and reign forever
The words authenticated; 'I am coming soon'; John forbidden to worship the angel
Do not seal the book; the time is near; blessing and exclusion
Jesus' self-testimony; the Spirit and the bride say 'Come'
Warning against adding to or taking from the prophecy
'Yes, I am coming soon.' 'Come, Lord Jesus!' The grace benediction

The opening verses finish the New Jerusalem vision by returning to Genesis 2-3. The Bible's story began with a garden watered by a river, a tree of life, and the presence of God, lost under the curse; it ends with all three restored and expanded into a city. John merges Eden with Ezekiel 47, where a river flows from the temple, deepening as it goes, turning the Dead Sea fresh, lined with trees that bear fruit every month and leaves for healing, and with Zechariah 14:8, where living waters flow out of Jerusalem. Jewish tradition had already linked these: 1 Enoch 24-25 describes the tree of life to be transplanted to the temple for the righteous; 4 Ezra 8:52 promises paradise and the tree of life to the righteous; Testament of Levi 18:10-11 says the messianic priest will open paradise and give the saints to eat of the tree of life. At the Feast of Tabernacles priests poured out water drawn from Siloam at the altar, a rite associated in later tradition with Ezekiel's river and the outpouring of the Spirit — the setting of Jesus' cry in John 7:37-39.

The epilogue (22:6-21) mirrors the prologue (1:1-8): the revelation given through an angel 'to show his servants what must soon take place', a blessing on those who keep its words, the titles Alpha and Omega, and the promise of Christ's coming. It closes in letter form with a grace benediction, as befits a circular letter to the seven churches to be read aloud in worship (1:3, 11). Its warning formula echoes Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32 and resembles the curses that ancient authors, treaty-makers and inscriptions placed against anyone altering a text (the Letter of Aristeas 310-311 pronounces a curse on revising the Greek Torah). The cry 'Come, Lord Jesus' renders in Greek the Aramaic prayer marana tha, preserved by Paul (1 Corinthians 16:22) and in the eucharistic prayers of the Didache (10:6). The epilogue's time texts ('soon', 'the time is near', 'I am coming soon') are central to the debate between preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist readings, and the dating of the book (before AD 70 or c. AD 95, disputed) bears directly on how they are read.
A river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb

A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden (Genesis 2:10-14). Ezekiel 47:1-12 sees water flowing from under the temple threshold, deepening into a river that brings life wherever it goes; Joel 3:18 and Zechariah 14:8 promise living waters from Jerusalem; Psalm 46:4 speaks of a river whose streams make glad the city of God. At Tabernacles, water from the Pool of Siloam was poured at the altar (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9, compiled c. AD 200), a rite later linked to Ezekiel's river.

Roman cities prized aqueducts and public fountains; Laodicea's lukewarm, mineral-laden piped water (3:15-16) contrasted with Hierapolis' hot springs and Colossae's cold water. A crystal-clear river flowing through a city was the ideal of urban luxury.

Eternal life flows directly from the shared throne of God and the Lamb. John 7:37-39 links the living water with the Spirit, and many see that connection here. The single throne of 'God and the Lamb' is a striking expression of Christ's full divine status.
Chilton and other partial preterists see the river flowing already through the church in the gospel and the Spirit's life, healing the nations through history, with its fullness at the consummation.
Futurists understand a real river in the eternal city (some dispensationalists also expect Ezekiel's river literally in the millennium), with spiritual significance.
Idealists and amillennialists read the river as the life of God given by the Spirit to his people, enjoyed in part now and perfectly in the new creation.
Down the middle of the main street of the city
Tobit 13:17-18 pictures Jerusalem's streets paved with precious stones and echoing with hallelujahs. Zechariah 8:4-5 envisions old men and children filling the streets of a restored Jerusalem.
Hellenistic cities were often organised around a broad colonnaded main street (plateia), the centre of commerce and civic life, such as the Arcadian Way and Curetes Street in Ephesus.

The river runs through the public heart of the city, so that the life of God shapes all its common life. The same word is used for the street where the two witnesses' bodies lay in the hostile city (11:8).
On either side of the river stood a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit… a fresh crop each month

The tree of life in Eden (Genesis 2:9) was barred after the fall by cherubim and a flaming sword (Genesis 3:22-24). Ezekiel 47:12: fruit trees along the river bearing every month. 1 Enoch 24:4-25:6 describes a fragrant tree to be transplanted to the temple for the righteous after the judgment; 4 Ezra 8:52 and Testament of Levi 18:11 promise access to the tree of life; Psalms of Solomon 14:3 compares the righteous to trees of life. Proverbs uses the tree of life for wisdom (Proverbs 3:18).

Colin Hemer proposed that the promise to Ephesus (2:7) plays on the sacred tree-shrine and asylum of Artemis at Ephesus; this connection is suggestive but debated. The Greek word xylon ('wood, tree') was also used by early Christians for the cross (Acts 5:30; 1 Peter 2:24).

Fulfils the promise to the overcomer at Ephesus (2:7): what Adam lost is restored. 'Tree' is probably collective (a grove lining both banks). Twelve fruits in twelve months mean perpetual, abundant provision; the number twelve ties the tree to the people of God.
The leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations

Ezekiel 47:12: the leaves are for healing. Isaiah 2:2-4 and 60:3 picture nations streaming to Zion; Isaiah 53:5 links healing to the Servant's wounds; Malachi 4:2 speaks of the sun of righteousness rising with healing.
Asia Minor was famous for healing cults — the Asclepieion at Pergamum, the medical school at Laodicea with its eye salve (3:18). The true healing of the nations comes from God's tree, not Asclepius.

John universalises Ezekiel by adding 'of the nations'. Why healing is needed in a world without pain raises the question whether this describes the present effects of the gospel, the restoration of national life, or simply the fullness of life in the new creation.
Postmillennialists see the healing of the nations as a process already under way through the gospel's progressive triumph in history, flowing into the final state.
Partial preterists (Chilton) read it as the church's present ministry to the nations since the new covenant was fully inaugurated.
Dispensationalists (Walvoord) take the leaves as sustaining the abundant life and health of the nations in the eternal state, not curing disease.
Amillennialists usually see a picture of the complete restoration of humanity from every nation, the curse's effects reversed forever.
No longer will there be any curse

The curse on the ground and on humanity after the fall (Genesis 3:14-19); Zechariah 14:11 promises that Jerusalem will dwell securely and there will be no more 'ban' or curse (herem, devotion to destruction).
Everything lost in Genesis 3 is reversed. The phrase also echoes Zechariah: the city will never again be devoted to destruction, unlike Babylon.
They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads

Moses was told no one could see God's face and live (Exodus 33:20); the priestly blessing prays that the LORD make his face shine on his people (Numbers 6:24-26); the psalmists long to behold his face (Psalm 17:15; 27:4; 42:2). The high priest wore a gold plate on his forehead engraved 'Holy to the LORD' (Exodus 28:36-38); Aaron's blessing put God's name on Israel (Numbers 6:27).

Slaves and soldiers were sometimes branded or tattooed with the owner's or commander's name; devotees of some cults bore marks of their god. The mark of the beast on forehead or hand (13:16) is the counterfeit.

The beatific vision: the highest privilege of Israel's high priest, once a year behind a veil, becomes the permanent privilege of all God's servants. The name on the forehead marks belonging, priestly holiness and transformation into his likeness (1 John 3:2).
The Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever
Daniel 7:18, 27: the saints of the Most High receive the kingdom forever and ever. Numbers 6:25 ('the LORD make his face shine upon you'). Isaiah 60:19-20.
The thousand-year reign of 20:4-6 gives way to — or is subsumed into — an everlasting reign. Humanity's original commission to rule creation (Genesis 1:26-28) is restored under God.
To show His servants what must soon take place

Daniel 2:28-29, 45 (Septuagint/Theodotion) speaks of what must take place 'in the last days' / 'after these things'; Revelation 1:1 and 22:6 reuse the phrase but change it to 'soon' (en tachei), suggesting that what Daniel saw as distant has now drawn near. 'The God of the spirits of the prophets' recalls Numbers 16:22 and 27:16 ('God of the spirits of all flesh') and 1 Enoch's title 'Lord of spirits'.

Bracketing the book with 1:1, the verse affirms the trustworthiness and prophetic authority of everything John has seen. The interpretation of 'soon' is a key dividing line between the major approaches.

Partial preterists (Gentry, Chilton) argue that 'soon' and 'near' must be taken at face value for the original readers, so that most of the book's prophecies (the judgment of Jerusalem and Rome's persecuting power) were fulfilled in the first century; the final chapters (20:7-22:5) still reach beyond to the end.

Full preterists (Russell, Preston) hold that 'soon' governs everything in the book, including Christ's coming, the resurrection and the new creation, all fulfilled by AD 70. Critics, including partial preterists, reply that Revelation itself places the final state after a long 'thousand years', and that this view denies the creedal future return; proponents answer that the thousand years is symbolic and fell within that generation.
Futurists explain en tachei as 'quickly/suddenly' once events begin, or as prophetic imminence measured by God's timescale (2 Peter 3:8-9); the events themselves remain largely future.
Historicists understand 'soon' to mean that the chain of fulfilment would begin promptly in John's day and unfold through church history to the end.

Idealists and amillennialists (Beale) read 'soon' as inaugurated eschatology: the last days began with Christ's resurrection, so the end is always near and the book's realities are always pressing upon the church.
Behold, I am coming soon

Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11: the Lord GOD comes with might, his reward with him. Malachi 3:1 (the Lord will suddenly come to his temple). Habakkuk 2:3 (the vision will surely come and not delay), a text Hebrews 10:37 applies to Christ's coming.
The parousia ('arrival') of an emperor or governor to a city was a public event prepared for with ceremony; Christians used the same word for Christ's coming.

Spoken three times in the epilogue (22:7, 12, 20), Jesus' promise is the book's final word of hope and warning. Coming 'soon' was also threatened to the churches (2:5, 16; 3:11), where it describes a conditional coming in judgment or help within the readers' lifetimes, which complicates reading every 'coming' as the final Parousia.

Partial preterists distinguish Christ's judgment-comings in history (to the churches, against Jerusalem in AD 70) from his final bodily return; the 'soon' in Revelation refers chiefly to the former, while the book still points to the latter.
Full preterists see one coming of Christ, fulfilled in AD 70 within the lifetime of John's readers.
Futurists see the promise of the personal, bodily Second Coming, imminent in the sense that it could occur at any time and will come suddenly.
Idealists hear both Christ's constant coming to his church in blessing and judgment and the final Parousia toward which all history moves.
Blessed is the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book
Blessings on those who keep God's words fill Deuteronomy (e.g. 28:1-14) and the Psalms (Psalm 1; 119:1-2).
Revelation was designed to be read aloud in the assembly (1:3); 'keeping' implies obeying and persevering, not merely decoding.
The sixth of seven beatitudes, echoing the first (1:3). The purpose of the prophecy is faithful endurance, not speculation.
I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel… 'Do not do that!… Worship God!'
As in 19:10, the angel's refusal reflects the Jewish conviction, shared with texts like the Ascension of Isaiah 7:21, that angels are fellow servants and must not be worshipped.
Angel veneration is attested in Phrygia and the Lycus valley (compare Colossians 2:18).

The repetition of 19:10 is deliberate: even an apostle-prophet can be dazzled into misplaced worship. Prophets and all who keep the book are fellow servants with angels; worship belongs to God (and, in Revelation, to the Lamb).
Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near

Daniel was told to shut up and seal his words until the time of the end (Daniel 8:26; 12:4, 9), because the fulfilment was far off. Apocalypses often claimed to be sealed writings hidden for a later generation (e.g., 1 Enoch 1:2; 4 Ezra 12:37-38; 14:44-47).
Documents were sealed to secure them until an authorised opening; an unsealed letter was meant to be read now.

A deliberate reversal of Daniel: what Daniel sealed is now opened because the time has arrived. 'The time is near' repeats 1:3. Preterists regard this contrast as among the strongest arguments for an early fulfilment of much of the book; others read it as marking the arrival of the last days, so it is variously interpreted.

Partial preterists note that Daniel's prophecy, about 400 years from fulfilment, was sealed; Revelation, by contrast, is unsealed, implying fulfilment for its first readers (the AD 60s on an early date).
Futurists reply that 'unsealed' means the message is now to be read and understood, since the last days have begun, not that every event will occur in the first century.
Idealists see the unsealing as the opening of the 'last days' with Christ's resurrection: the book applies to every generation of the church.
Let the unrighteous continue to be unrighteous… let the holy continue to be holy
Daniel 12:10: many will be purified and made white, but the wicked will continue in wickedness. Ezekiel 3:27 ('he who will hear, let him hear; he who refuses, let him refuse').
Not a counsel of indifference but an urgent warning: the time is short, and people are confirming their character. Like the 'he who has ears' formula, it calls for decision while there is time.
My reward is with Me, to give to each one according to what he has done
Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11 (his reward is with him); Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12 (God repays each according to his work); Jeremiah 17:10.
Christ himself takes on the divine role of judge and rewarder, assigned to God in Isaiah. The note of judgment by works matches 20:12-13.
I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End
Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12: the LORD, Israel's King and Redeemer, is the first and the last, besides whom there is no God.
Greek magical and philosophical texts used alphabet symbolism for cosmic totality; John uses it for the God of Israel.

All three titles are combined here and placed on the lips of Jesus. 'Alpha and Omega' and 'Beginning and End' were used of God (1:8; 21:6) and 'First and Last' of Christ (1:17; 2:8); now all belong to Jesus, one of the clearest assertions in the New Testament that he shares the identity of the one God (Bauckham).
Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates

Israel washed their garments to prepare to meet God at Sinai (Exodus 19:10, 14); priests washed before entering the sanctuary (Exodus 29:4; 40:12); Zechariah 3:3-5 has filthy garments removed from the high priest. Psalm 24:3-4 asks who may ascend the hill of the LORD.

The seventh and final beatitude. Robes washed in the blood of the Lamb (7:14) give access to the tree of life — Eden's barrier is lifted. A textual variant (in the Byzantine manuscripts followed by the KJV) reads 'do his commandments' instead of 'wash their robes'; the earlier manuscripts support 'wash their robes'.
